title: Separate 'is the service down' from 'is the name wrong'
explanation: The service and its name are two independent things that can each fail on their own. `curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/` succeeding while `curl http://api.internal:8080/` fails to connect proves the app itself is fine — whatever's broken happens before the request ever leaves this host, in how `api.internal` gets turned into an address.

title: See what the name actually resolves to
explanation: `getent hosts api.internal` asks the same resolution path the C library (and therefore `curl`) actually uses, rather than guessing. It returns `10.99.99.99` — an address that isn't this machine at all, which is why the connection attempt goes nowhere.

title: Know why a static file can silently override real DNS
explanation: Per `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, name resolution on Linux checks `/etc/hosts` before ever querying DNS (the default `hosts: files dns` order). A stale line in `/etc/hosts` doesn't fail loudly or get overridden by correct DNS records elsewhere — it just wins, every time, silently, because it's consulted first.

title: Editing a bind-mounted file needs an in-place tool
explanation: Inside a container, `/etc/hosts` is bind-mounted from the runtime, not a normal file in the image's own filesystem. Tools like `sed -i` work by writing a new file and renaming it over the old one — but you can't rename over a bind-mounted inode, so they fail with 'Device or resource busy'. An in-place editor like `nano`, or a copy-back (`cat > /etc/hosts` or `cp /tmp/h /etc/hosts`), writes into the existing file instead and succeeds.

title: Verify with the same lookup that first exposed the bug
explanation: Re-running `curl http://api.internal:8080/` (not just `getent hosts` again) confirms the fix end-to-end — the name now resolves to `127.0.0.1` and the request that a real client would make actually succeeds.
